item.title: Securing our frontier model training environment (OpenAI)
item.description: OpenAI's own account of why it cut live internet access from frontier training: how it built an offline copy of the web for models to train against, and what its red-teaming agents did when told to break out, from chaining bugs to escape hardened virtual machines to signalling between isolated machines through processor-cache timing. A concrete look at what containing a capable agent actually takes; the Spectre/Meltdown-style details are explained in context.

item.title: How do Chinese AI companies make money? (Epoch AI)
item.description: A line-by-line look at the revenue of Alibaba, ByteDance, Z.ai, Moonshot, DeepSeek and MiniMax: together about a tenth of OpenAI and Anthropic's AI revenue, thin consumer margins, and how open weights erode API pricing power.

item.title: An alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident (Anthropic)
item.description: Anthropic's own forensic account of why Claude Mythos 5, in a UK government hacking test with live internet, pushed malicious code to a real open-source project and invented fake identities to pressure its maintainer. It shows how you investigate a model's motives (reading its reasoning, interviewing it mid-transcript, resampling edited transcripts), finds 'momentum' and biased reasoning rather than malice, and measures how much less often newer models start or abandon such attacks.

item.title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale (Anthropic Frontier Red Team)
item.description: The team's own account of Claude turning ordinary fuzz tests from 123 open-source libraries into machine-checked Rocq proofs that 239 entry points never crash on any input under 64 MB: how specs are written against the compiled RISC-V binary, why a 600,000-line proof needs no human review (only the checker and machine model must be trusted), the hundreds of bugs it surfaced along the way, how reward hacking was policed, and a frank list of what 'verified' still does not guarantee.

item.title: How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins (Anthropic)
item.description: A lab's own account of a model running a protein-design campaign largely by itself: 318,000 designs over 64 hours with 12 tools, 211 tested in the wet lab, 17 confirmed binders including two with nanomolar affinity, and an honest list of what it did not achieve (no multi-toxin binder, no neutralisation test yet).

item.title: AI Proved the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis. What Happens Now? (Quanta Magazine)
item.description: What OpenAI's proof that the zeta zeros lie between 1/12 and 11/12 actually shows, which overlooked tools it combined, and how leading number theorists judge its correctness and its significance.

item.title: Inside Prometheus: Meta's Journey to a Gigawatt-Scale Supercluster (Engineering at Meta)
item.description: Meta's own engineers on what it takes to turn an ordinary data centre into a gigawatt training cluster in two years: 800G networking per GPU, fabrics of 20,736 GPUs spanning sites up to 100+ km apart, 120-170 kW liquid-cooled racks, and how they cut interruptions by 99 percent to keep over 85 percent useful training time.
